body: Over the next three weeks, contractors will carry out the following work in the building. Please read this notice carefully, as some of the work will affect access to your flat.
## Lift

The main lift will be out of service from Monday 3 March to Friday 7 March while its motor is replaced. The stairs will remain open. Residents who cannot use the stairs should contact the building manager by 28 February so that assistance can be arranged.
## Water
The cold water supply will be switched off on Tuesday 11 March between 9 am and 1 pm for pipe repairs. Please fill any containers you need before 9 am. Hot water will not be affected.
## Windows
External window cleaning will take place on 18 and 19 March. Cleaners will use a platform on the outside of the building; please close your windows and remove items from window sills on those days.
## Car park
Bays 1–12 will be repainted on Friday 21 March. Cars parked in these bays after 8 am will be moved at the owner's expense.
## Noise
Drilling will be limited to 9 am – 5 pm on weekdays. There will be no work at weekends.
Questions should be directed to the building manager, Ms Okafor, on 0161 496 0742 or at manager@maplecourt.example, not to the contractors.

body: The market takes place on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, from 8 am to 1 pm, in the square outside the town hall. It runs all year, except when the fourth Saturday falls on 25 December.
## Who can sell
Producers only. Everything on your stall must be grown, reared, baked or made by you within 40 miles of the town. We do not accept resellers, and we visit each producer before their first market.
## Fees

A standard stall (3 metres) costs £25 per market. A half stall costs £15. Electricity is available for an extra £5 and must be requested when you book, as there are only ten sockets. New stallholders pay for their first three markets in advance; after that, fees are paid on the day.
## Setting up

Vehicles may enter the square from 6.30 am and must leave by 7.45 am. No vehicles are allowed in the square during trading hours. You must bring your own table and gazebo, and every gazebo must be weighted down: we have had accidents in windy weather.
## Rules
Prices must be clearly displayed. Food sellers must hold a current hygiene certificate and show it on request. Please take all rubbish away with you; the council does not collect market waste.
To apply, complete the form on our website. Applications are reviewed once a month.
texts.label: B

headings.text: Early theories and the first discoveries
How the sound was recorded for the first time
A sound reported across the world

paragraphs.text: Travellers crossing the deserts of Asia and Arabia have reported it for centuries: a deep, humming note that rises from the dunes without any obvious cause. Marco Polo wrote of sands that seemed to fill the air with the sounds of musical instruments. In some places the sound resembles a distant aircraft, in others a cello or a foghorn, and it can last for several minutes and be heard several kilometres away. Only around forty dunes in the world are known to sing, among them dunes in China, Chile, Morocco, Oman and the United States, and for a long time the phenomenon was treated as a curiosity rather than a subject for science. Sailors, too, have described a similar booming from the beaches of certain islands, and desert peoples have their own names for it. The sound is loud enough to be felt as a vibration through the feet, and early visitors sometimes mistook it for thunder.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: For a long time nobody could say what produced the sound. Early explanations involved wind blowing across the crests, hollow spaces beneath the sand, or even spirits living inside the dunes. In the twentieth century researchers established the first solid facts. The note is produced not by the wind but by the sand itself, when a large quantity of it slides down the steep face of a dune. A person sliding down on their back can set it off, and so can a small avalanche started by the wind. Dunes that sing are always dry and always made of grains of roughly equal size, polished smooth by long exposure to the wind. Wet sand, or sand mixed with grains of different sizes, never sings, however steep the slope.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The mechanism, as far as it is understood, is one of synchronisation. When a layer of sand begins to flow, the grains collide with one another and with the stationary sand beneath. Each collision produces a tiny vibration. In ordinary sand these vibrations are random and cancel each other out. In singing sand, because the grains are so similar in size, they begin to bounce in step, like soldiers marching, and their combined vibration is loud enough to hear. The frequency of the note depends on the size of the grains: larger grains produce a lower note. This is why one dune in Morocco always sings the same pitch, close to G sharp, while a dune in Oman produces a note almost an octave higher. The size of the sliding layer matters too: a small trickle of sand produces only a faint hum, while a large avalanche can be heard from a distance. Experiments in which sand is made to slide in a laboratory have confirmed that the whole flowing layer vibrates as a single body.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Yet mysteries remain. Some dunes that appear to have every necessary quality stay silent, and a singing dune can lose its voice after rain and recover it weeks later. In laboratory experiments, sand taken from a singing dune sings in a rotating drum, but only if it is dried and left for a while; freshly washed grains produce nothing. Researchers suspect that a thin coating on each grain, built up over years of exposure, is what allows the grains to move together, and that moisture destroys it. If they are right, the song of the dunes is not only a matter of physics but also a record of the desert's history. Others suspect that the answer lies deeper, in the way moisture changes the density of the sand below the surface, and the debate is likely to continue for some years.
paragraphs.label: D

RECEPTIONIST: Clayworks Studio, good morning.
ANNA: Hello, I'm interested in the beginners' pottery course. Could you tell me a bit about it?
RECEPTIONIST: Of course. It runs on Wednesday evenings from seven to nine, for six weeks. The next one starts on the third of October… no, I'm looking at the old list — it's the tenth of October.

RECEPTIONIST: Eight, so it's quite small. There are three places left at the moment.

RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. And an email address?

clips.context: A bus company announcement about a temporary route change.
clips.transcript: This is an announcement for passengers using the number 22 bus. From Monday the seventh of March, the route will change while the bridge on River Road is being repaired. Buses will no longer stop at the hospital; instead, they will go along Park Avenue and stop outside the sports centre, which is about a five-minute walk from the hospital entrance. The journey into town will take around ten minutes longer, so please allow extra time. Evening buses after nine o'clock are not affected, as the bridge will be open to traffic at night. clips.context: Two students plan a survey of food waste in campus canteens.
clips.transcript:
LUCAS: Right, Sofia, we need to decide how we're actually going to collect the data on food waste in the canteens.
SOFIA: I still think a questionnaire is the easiest. We can hand it out at lunchtime.
LUCAS: The problem is that people say what they think they do, not what they actually do. Everybody claims they never waste food.
SOFIA: True. So what — we stand by the bins and watch?
LUCAS: Not watch, weigh. The canteen staff already separate the food waste. If we weigh the bins at the end of each day for two weeks, we get real numbers.
SOFIA: That's a lot more work, but the data would be much stronger. Could we do both? Weigh the bins and ask a short questionnaire about why people leave food?
LUCAS: That's a good compromise. Keep the questionnaire to five questions, though, or nobody will fill it in.
SOFIA: Agreed. Now, which canteens? There are four on campus.
LUCAS: I'd say just the two big ones. The small ones only do sandwiches, so there's hardly any waste to measure.
SOFIA: OK. And we should speak to the catering manager first — we can't just start weighing her bins.
LUCAS: I emailed her yesterday. She's happy, as long as we share the results, because they've been trying to reduce waste anyway.
SOFIA: Great. Then the timeline: two weeks of data from the fourteenth, analysis in the week after, and the presentation on the fourth of the following month.

clips.context: Part of a lecture on desert beetles that collect fog.
clips.transcript: Good afternoon. Today we move from plants to insects, and to one of the most elegant solutions to water shortage that nature has produced. The Namib Desert on the coast of south-west Africa receives almost no rain — in some years less than ten millimetres — yet it is home to a surprising range of animals. What it does have is fog. On many mornings, cold air from the Atlantic rolls inland and covers the dunes for a few hours. One species of beetle has learned to harvest it. Before dawn, the beetle climbs to the top of a dune, faces into the wind and tilts its body forward, raising its back into the air. The surface of its back is covered with tiny bumps. The tops of these bumps attract water, while the smooth areas between them repel it. Droplets of fog collect on the bumps, grow until they are heavy enough to move, and then roll down the water-repelling channels straight into the beetle's mouth. In effect, the insect drinks by standing still. Engineers have copied this design to make fog-collecting nets and even self-filling water bottles, and the same idea is being tested for cooling the surfaces of buildings. What interests me most, though, is not the technology but the lesson: in a place where the obvious resource is absent, survival depends on noticing the one that is there.
